Since the Montreal regional council of the Public Service Alliance of Canada has declared its determination to continue boycotting the second language as long as the Treasury Board refuses to respect its promise to pay a bilingualism bonus; since the government has repeatedly stated formally that it considers it fair and equitable to pay that bonus; since an increasing number of federal civil servants in Quebec intend to ask that their jobs now classified as bilingual be reclassified as unilingual because, to quote them almost textually, they are fed up with claiming compensation they are being denied; and since it is imperative that the citizens being served by the civil servants
concerned should have the choice of either official language in this country, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey):

subsubtopic: OUTFLOW OF CAPITAL FROM CANADA-EFFECT OF REVIEW PROCEDURES-ESTIMATE OF NUMBER OF JOBS LOST
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. The Bank of Canada has revealed that in the last four years there has been an acceleration of Canadian direct investment abroad and a deceleration of foreign investments here, so that in 1976 there was a net outflow of nearly $1 billion, costing tens of thousands of Canadian jobs. Would the Prime Minister indicate if his administration anticipated such a turnaround when it introduced its foreign investment review procedures, bearing in mind that such a flight of capital has resulted not only in higher unemployment but also in a brain drain of some of our most talented people?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: OUTFLOW OF CAPITAL FROM CANADA-EFFECT OF REVIEW PROCEDURES-ESTIMATE OF NUMBER OF JOBS LOST
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the least I can say is that the question is extremely complex. Certainly, the Foreign Investment Review Agency did have as its stated objective screening investment so that it would be allowed only when it brings significant benefit to Canada. I would be surprised if the hon. member would disagree with that. As far as Canadian capital being invested elsewhere is concerned, there are no exchange controls on the Canadian dollar, and the Canadian investor is free to invest wherever he will get the maximum return for his dollar.

subsubtopic: OUTFLOW OF CAPITAL FROM CANADA-EFFECT OF REVIEW PROCEDURES-ESTIMATE OF NUMBER OF JOBS LOST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to explore this subject a little further with the Prime Minister. Faced with an

8 per cent unemployment level at the present time and the anticipation that it might go even higher-in fact, it is now at a higher level than any major industrialized country-would the Prime Minister go further and indicate to what extent his foreign investment review procedures or other related government policies have contributed to unemployment by discouraging foreign investment and job creation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: OUTFLOW OF CAPITAL FROM CANADA-EFFECT OF REVIEW PROCEDURES-ESTIMATE OF NUMBER OF JOBS LOST
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must repeat in part my previous answer. Foreign investment continues to be welcome in Canada, but only if it brings significant benefit. This, of course, includes the creation of jobs. It is on that basis that a great deal of foreign investment has continued to be allowed over the past several years since the creation of the Foreign Investment Review Agency. If the hon. member checks the figures, he will see that it is a small proportion indeed of foreign investment which is screened out, and one of the considerations of the review agency is to see if the investment will bring jobs or not. In the latter case, the investment is not encouraged unless there are other benefits.

subsubtopic: OUTFLOW OF CAPITAL FROM CANADA-EFFECT OF REVIEW PROCEDURES-ESTIMATE OF NUMBER OF JOBS LOST
speechtext: With almost daily press reports of further Canadian investment in foreign lands, would the Prime Minister tell the House whether he is concerned about this trend or, at least, would he indicate if he has received any report on this apparent exodus of money, know-how and jobs, and if so, could he estimate how many jobs have been lost so far?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: OUTFLOW OF CAPITAL FROM CANADA-EFFECT OF REVIEW PROCEDURES-ESTIMATE OF NUMBER OF JOBS LOST
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. I have not received any report on this nor an estimate of jobs lost so far, but the facts the hon. member raises are facts of which we are aware, and they change from time to time. There is a period in the cycle when members of parliament complain that there is too much foreign investment, and at other times they complain that there is too much Canadian investment going abroad. We have always taken the view that the economy should function in such a way that investors in normal times can be free to seek the best possible return for their dollar, and if that is not the case in Canada, that means we have to manage our economy better and increase our productivity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday, June 9, the hon. member for New Westminster put a question to the Solicitor General regarding the evidence given before a judicial inquiry in Edmonton in relation to a charge that RCMP officers had illegally bugged the hotel rooms of three Edmonton police officers. At that time the Solicitor General said that the Deputy Commissioner of the RCMP had been delegated by the commissioner to investigate the matter and that he found there was no bugging. The minister's statement is completely at variance with an evidence given to the Laycraft Inquiry yesterday reported in yesterday's Globe and Mail as follows:
The inquiry also heard Assistant Commissioner Peter Wright, head of the RCMP in Alberta testify that Ross Paisley, Alberta's deputy attorney-general told him that the bugging was "a fact," not "an allegation," and that Assistant Commissioner George Paquette, in charge of the RCMP in Manitoba at the time of the bugging, had approved it.
Has the minister been in touch with the deputy attorney general of Alberta, to determine if the assertions the deputy commissioner of the RCMP made on the stand are accurate? More especially, has the Solicitor General been in touch with Assistant Commissioner Paquette, to determine if he approved the bugging?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. UPGRADING OF PRAIRIE RAIL NETWORK-REASON FOR FAILURE TO PROVIDE AMOUNT OF MONEY PROMISED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Transport. The Hall Commission recommended an amount in excess of $445 million for the rehabilitation and upgrading of the prairie rail network, and on May 27 the minister said in Regina that in the period immediately ahead there would be a firm commitment of $200 million to start the railways on this program of rehabilitation and upgrading. Yesterday, however, the minister announced in Calgary that the sum of $100 million would be provided. I should like to ask him what happened to the other $100 million he gave a firm commitment to provide in Regina in May. Can the hon. gentleman assure the House that he will not accept any excuse from the railroads that they can only spend $100 million during the period envisaged, because I can assure him that there are private companies which are able and willing to carry out some of this work?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: UPGRADING OF PRAIRIE RAIL NETWORK-REASON FOR FAILURE TO PROVIDE AMOUNT OF MONEY PROMISED
speechtext: I welcome the hon. member back to the House, but I must say I regret his selective quoting, in the course of which he left out the important word "seeking". The initial commitment of $100 million is intended to accommodate the construction and rehabilitation work which can be accomplished in the construction years 1977 and 1978. It is, however, an extremely constructive step and a maximum move forward in further commitment following the recommendations of the Hall commission. I think hon. members, particularly those from the west, should appreciate the willingness of the government to commit $100 million for this purpose at this time of serious fiscal restraint.

CROWSNEST PASS RATES-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF MINISTER'S STATEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we welcome the $100 million but we would welcome more the commitment from the minister to implement the recommendation of the Hall report, which will amount to about five times that which he is talking about at the moment. The minister also said in Calgary, to quote from the press, that "the west should consider if it would not be better served by having the Crow benefit paid in a more neutral way". What does the minister mean by that statement, since the west has already considered how it wants the benefits of the Crow rate applied? The recommendations of the Hall commission have been accepted and agreed to by the wheat pools and the prairie governments. Would the minister explain what he means by "a neutral way", and will he say whether the government accepts the recommendation of Mr. Justice Hall about the retention of the Crow rate and the payment direct to the railroads of any losses on grain hauling?

Mr. Speaker, our approach to rehabilitation evidences a willingness to move

along those lines. I will send the hon. member several previous speeches of mine which analyse the alternative ways that the Crow rate will be paid. As the hon. member may know, from the western point of view I do not consider this matter closed. I have said, and I said again in that Calgary speech, that I considered it my obligation as a minister representing the west to attempt to persuade the government about the amount of money required to ensure the Crow rate for the west and the benefit of that rate, and that I will continue to do and I make that known at all times. FREIGHT RATES-REQUEST FOR CHANGE IN RATE ON RAPESEED PRODUCTS
speechtext: A final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. It is obvious to all but the minister that the west has accepted the Hall commission recommendation on the Crow rates. That is the position of my party and certainly it is what the wheat pools and the prairie governments feel. The Hall commission recommended that freight rates on rapeseed and its derivatives be set at levels which do not discriminate against the natural location advantage of rapeseed crushers in the west. By recommending retention of the Crowsnest rates the commission has, by implication, recommended that the inequity discriminating against western rapeseed crushers be resolved by lowering the freight rate on rapeseed products. When will the minister act on this recommendation and when will the necessary changes be made to have rapeseed products qualify for lower freight rates?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-REQUEST FOR CHANGE IN RATE ON RAPESEED PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hall commission did recommend a good number of things in regard to freight rates and products. It also said that the question whether the statutory Crow rates should be set at a particular level or at some other level is something that ought to be decided by the government; and obviously that did not answer a question but opened a question.
In relation to grain products moving out of the west there is a very serious issue, which again I raised in my speech in Calgary, namely that the only alternative to inequity in the west against processing which is produced by the low grain rate is the putting of all kinds of other products on a similar low rate. That was not quantified by the commission, but probably if you include western movement of meat and other products, presumably by trucks as well as by rail, this amounts to many hundreds of millions of dollars. In addition, I am not sure whether the hon. member is suggesting that there would be a way to put that low meat rate in place in the west without

HYPERLIPEMIA-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ASSESS MEANS OF CONTROL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, regarding a question which I asked on July 7, 1977 as reported at page 7414 of Hansard. As was stated at that time, the minister gave an address in Vancouver to a professional group of doctors and nurses which covered the field very well, except the field of scientific work. At that time the minister said the following:
... there is no consensus within the medical profession on the usefulness or cost effectiveness of a nation-wide screening program for children.
It is an accepted fact that they are doing lipid profiles on people in labs all across Canada. They have even been done on children. If we are going to effectively treat this disease, we must get those cases early. Now they are doing testing from 20 years of age on. Why not return to the starting point, because once cardiovascular disease is established little can be done about its cure. It is progressive.
This should be carried on as a public health program. After all, he was talking to public health doctors and nurses. Why

should this not be carried on as a public health program or a pre-school examination which is already paid for? They could have their blood tested at that time. One must keep in mind that some of those lipid diseases are hereditary. Some would be picked up there and others would be picked up as well, thus reducing the terrible mortality he referred to.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: HYPERLIPEMIA-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ASSESS MEANS OF CONTROL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the view of my department, children with a known strong family history of hyperlipemia should be investigated at different levels. The question arises as to the general screening for children. I have noted the suggestion made by the hon. member. I will investigate the matter further with provincial officials, and I will ask my officials to examine it with them as well, in order to determine the advisability of extending such a project. As I told him before, it would have to be started as a pilot project rather than as a national program. It is a matter which deserves investigation, indeed.

maintopic: HYPERLIPEMIA-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ASSESS MEANS OF CONTROL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the minister believes in prevention, would he suggest this as part of a pre-school examination.
It does not have to be a pilot project, it has to be a pre-school examination because otherwise it would take too long. Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which has to do with questions on the order paper standing in the name of my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East, which were answered on July 15, which answers are misleading and certainly incomplete. The parliamentary secretary said categorically that no officers of CMHC were charged. The man charged and convicted was not an officer of the corporation, but the question was not whether any officer had been charged; it was whether an official had been charged. He was an official, he was charged and convicted, and he was sentenced to three months in jail and a fine of $2,000. The question was answered by the parliamentary secretary this afternoon in such a way as to mislead the House, just as the answer of the minister on July 15 misled the House.
July 19, 1977

With regard to question No. 12, the minister clearly evaded answering the question. I, as well as other members of the House, am clearly aware of the difference between direct loans and guaranteed loans under CMHC. The question was whether or not CMHC at all times was in a first mortgage position. The minister answered in a way that made it impossible for us to ascertain whether or not CMHC was, in fact, always in a first mortgage position. Philosophically, I recognize the absolute right of the government to govern, but to be able to fulfil my responsibilities as a member of parliament and to scrutinize the government, to criticize the government, indeed to act as a watchdog, 1 must be sure that answers to questions which are put on the order paper must at least not be misleading. I understand that I cannot question the quality of the answers- but I must be sure that they are not misleading.
Specifically speaking, question No. 16 on the order paper deliberately misleads the House. The question was whether CMHC is satisfied that all funds approved and advanced to York Place were actually used in York Place. comments heard by the reporter and not heard by those who have the floor and, in fact, never heard by the Chair. When they appear in the record the following day, therefore, they incline to give a distorted impression of the events that have taken place. Often, when no answer appears in the record to such comments, the impression is given that the person to whom the comment was directed has not taken any action in respect of it, when in fact the comment was not heard except by the reporter. Indeed, some hon. members who have positions close to the reporter are able to take advantage of that.
I am not so sure that the answer suggested by the hon. member for Moncton is any better than the situation which prevails at the present time. It does raise a very serious difficulty, however, in respect of those who may on occasion take advantage of the fact that the comment made audibly to the reporter, but not audibly to the person who has the floor or to the Chair, is recorded in Hansard and only comes to the attention of those persons the following day. If there is a suggestion to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization that we ought to revise our procedures and have reporters record only the remarks of the member who has the floor, that is something that I hope the committee would examine very carefully one day.

Those questions have not been answered since the first day of the session. I do not think it should take months and months to arrive at the answers.
I think I am within my rights to serve notice that when we come back in August-as I believe we have been told, but it is a good question as to whether we will-as a private member 1 will exercise my right to move the adjournment of the House if all the questions regarding the international service of the CBC, and the questions regarding cabinet ministers gallivanting at the taxpayers' expense are not answered. I refer to the ministers who went down to the riding of Matane. I have questions on the order paper about what they did there, why they did it, and how much it cost. We get nothing from the President of the Privy Council or his parliamentary secretary. I do not think this practice should be allowed to continue. I do not think we should be presented with silly generalities or hear hon. members opposite boast about how many questions they have answered.
I conclude by asking three questions. Perhaps the parliamentary secretary can answer. How long will this sham continue? How long will the government get away with stifling democracy by not answering questions in this House; and how

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I spoke on this legislation some days ago, I said that the bill, which proposes to deal with serious unemployment by making it more difficult for the unemployed to draw unemployment insurance benefits, seeks to apply the wrong solution to the wrong people. By dividing the country into 53 or 54 regions, in each of which claimants may qualify for benefits on the basis of different period of employment, the bill will create an administrative jungle.

I shall try to show this afternoon how the unemployment insurance bureaucracy treated-"mistreated" is a better description-a poor woman unfortunate enough to be unemployed. You can imagine how much greater the confusion will be with the administrative nightmare of 53 or 54 different areas. My involvement in the case was greater than usual. 1 discussed the case with the claimant and local officers in Winnipeg. Not being satisfied with the response, I discussed it with the chairman of the Unemployment Insurance Commission here in Ottawa. Although the operation was successful, the patient, my constituent, died. Of course, I am speaking figuratively about her dealing with the Unemployment Insurance Commission. I shall put on record certain facts to enable members of parliament and the public to know what happened. I want the officers of the commission to explain to the minister what they have not explained to me, namely, what actually happened, and to justify it.
My constituent, Mrs. Ruth Hirsch, is a social worker with a number of years experience in her field. Her most recent employment was with the family service organization of Winnipeg. She became unemployed when her agency was reorganized and her services were no longer required. She received unemployment insurance benefits for some weeks, then was called in for an interview with the benefit control officer who made a report of that so-called interview. I have in my possession a copy of what purports to be a complete file on the matter, a copy which I obtained from the chairman of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. I shall return later to the question as to whether it is the entire file and if it depicts the entire story. The benefit control officer, B. Kolisnyk, wrote a report on February 10, 1977, which said in part:
Claimant has a Bachelor in social work and a number of years experience. Claimant will work days only as she must be home evenings and for no less that $10,000/year. Claimant will work anywhere in Winnipeg. Claimant has not been sick or out of Winnipeg since filing her claim.
On February 15, Mr. W. Chimchak, an insurance officer wrote an official letter to Mrs. Ruth Hirsch as follows:
Dear Madam:
We find that you are not entitled to benefits from 14 Feb., '77, as you failed to prove that you are available for work and unable to obtain suitable employment in that, after being unemployed for a reasonable period, you are imposing restrictive conditions on your acceptance of suitable work in respect of the type of work (social worker or counsellor) you will accept.
Mrs. Hirsch replied immediately and on February 17 sent a letter to Mr. Chimchak, which said in part:
Re your letter of February 15/77, and further to our telephone conversation of today, I wish to appeal the decision that I am not entitled to benefits from Feb. 14/77.
As far as the "imposing restrictive conditions",
(1)	accepting work only as a social worker or counsellor. This, in fact, is not accurate. I am prepared to accept work that involves helping people (which may or may not be defined as a social worker or counsellor)-such as personnel officer, mental health worker, UIC interviewer, rehabilitation officer, mental retardation worker, etc., etc.
(2)	"re days only". 1 have 2 retarded school age children living at home, and therefore I must be home with at night. I am prepared to submit a report from their and/or my doctor(s) to that effect.
(3)	"re not less that $10,000 per annum". This was the salary of my last position. I am prepared to work for less.
July 19, 1977

She appealed the case, and the appeal board in its decision dated March 15, 1977, said in part:
She is still unemployed and still searching for work, but everything points to the fact that she is still restricting her search for work in the field of employment that deals with people. In other words, a form of social work for which she is trained and has experience, but in no way can this board find justification in altering the decision of the insurance officer, and the appeal is disallowed.
Mrs. Hirsch wanted to appeal to the office of the umpire. She got in touch with me and I suggested to her that she should make it clear the benefit control officer never informed her what kind of work she should look for. What would the commission consider to be suitable work? She stated in her appeal, and 1 quote:
At no time during my unemployment was I informed or encouraged to seek employment outside of my specialized field. As a matter of fact, 1 was asked to apply for a position with Canada Manpower. This I immediately did.
She went on to list some of the things she did. Her request for right to appeal was turned down in a letter dated April 20, which reads in part:
Your application for leave to appeal to the umpire from the decision of the board of referees given in Winnipeg, Manitoba, on 15 March, 1977, was forwarded to the chairman of the board of referees for his consideration.
We wish to inform you that the chairman has not approved your application for leave to appeal to the umpire-
I was pretty upset about this. 1 felt she had been mistreated.
I took the matter up with the local office and with Mr. Tuck, the chairman of the commission. Mr. Tuck wrote to me saying that Mrs. Hirsch was being given permission to have another hearing before the same appeal board. The appeal was held. I will come to that in a few minutes. She was turned down.
When I again raised my voice, I got what are purported to be copies of the complete file. Nowhere in the file is there any explanation as to why, having been refused permission to go to the umpire, she was permitted another appeal. There is no mention, in the supposedly complete record, that her member of parliament intervened on her behalf. I wonder why. I am not ashamed of the fact that I intervened. Maybe 1 was wrong, but I am happy to intervene when I think a person has a good case. If I do not think a person has a good case, I say that I cannot intervene or that I cannot do anything more. In any event, there is nothing in the record. I say the record is defective; it is incomplete.
In the course of my discussion with Mr. Tuck, I was assured again and again that benefit control officers clearly understand that they should be telling those whose claims are turned down or are being cut off what are their rights.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that is precisely what 1 am doing. In this bill the minister is proposing to divide the qualifying period of those entitled to receive unemployment insurance benefits: he proposes to divide the country into 54 districts, each of which will have a different qualifying period. One of the main reasons I intend to vote against this bill is that I believe the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Commission is incompetent, or the Unemployment Insurance Act and the regulations are deliberately being used by the commission, with or without the knowledge of the government, to reduce the number of people who qualify. That is precisely the point I am making.
I intend to prove my case by quoting from the guidelines under which Unemployment Insurance Commission employees are supposed to work. I have here a document entitled "Insurance policy guildelines, Conduct of the active job search program, Commission minute 73-144, August 1973''. 1 received this from Mr. Tuck, chairman of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. I want to put various parts of this on record in order to show what UIC officials should be doing, rather than the way they dealt with my constituent. I do not raise this matter because I think my constituent's case is an isolated one. In a letter I received last week, Mr. Tuck virtually admitted that this has been the policy of the government, and they are now changing it. I am not vain enough to believe they are changing it only because I raised the matter with them. I presume there have been many complaints.
1 will give the page numbers of the document so the minister and his officials can check them. I quote, first, from page 15-32, a draft letter, or to be used verbally when giving information to a claimant before being cut off by the benefit control officer:
You have been receiving unemployment insurance benefits now for a period
of

weeks. In order for you to maintain your eligibility for benefits, you
must now broaden your search to seek other suitable employment in any occupation... It is necessary, therefore, that you contact as many potential employers as possible to see if you are able to fill any vacancies in suitable employment that exist.
What is suitable? There is nothing in Mr. Tuck's letter to indicate that Mrs. Hirsch's claim is not valid. There is nothing in this document to indicate what is suitable employment. The benefit control officer did not tell Mrs. Hirsch what is suitable employment. 1 quote from page 16-32:
To find where jobs may be available, you should either check with your Canada Manpower centre and Canada job bank listings, search through newspaper advertisements, job posters, yellow pages of the telephone book or enquire from your friends, neighbours or the people with whom you used to work. You should contact possible employers by telephoning, writing, or visiting them to see if employment is available.
Mrs. Hirsch did all that. I now go to page 19-32, criteria for issue of job search statement. I quote:
No claimant will be required to search for work unless it is known that there are opportunities of employment in the area of his residence and/or in the area

July 19, 1977
Employment and Immigration
where he usually earns his living. The area of residence is intended to include the area within daily commuting distance.
I quote that section because the benefit control officer in her statement says that Mrs. Hirsch, restricted herself to looking for work in Winnipeg. Winnipeg is a big city. Do the UIC people believe that Mrs. Hirsch, or someone else, should travel 50 miles every day in order to fill a job? If so, they did not say that. I now quote from page 21:
Full advantage will be taken of this interview to ensure that the claimant is aware of his obligation to actively search for work and that he understands what in his circumstances would be considered a reasonable and customary effort.
There is no question in the documentation that Mrs. Hirsch was looking for work. She listed a series of places in which she had looked, including employment as a social worker and other places. If that was not broad enough, it was up to the UIC officer to tell her what was required. That is the position I have taken from the beginning.
On page 22, the document says a claimant is required to prove that he is capable of working and is available for work, that he is unable to find suitable employment and that he has made reasonable and customary efforts to find suitable employment. The question I want to ask is this: Who decides what is suitable employment? If it is the Unemployment Insurance Commission, then it is surely elementary justice to the claimant that the commission should be required to indicate the kind of work they expect a claimant, in this case Mrs. Hirsch, to take. If the commission felt she ought not to receive benefit because the work she wanted as a social worker, in the field of treating those mentally retarded, or as a personnel officer, was too restricted, it was surely up to those concerned to say to her, "You are restricting yourself too much. Instead of being prepared to work at those jobs for $10,000 a year"- which amounts to about $5 an hour-"you should be prepared to work as a filing clerk or as a dishwasher to earn, not $5 an hour but the minimum wage". But Mrs. Hirsch was not given such advice.
The guidelines go on to say that if a reasonable job search is not done, a person would be disqualified retroactively, notified of this decision in writing, and "informed of the manner in which the denial of benefits can be removed, that is to say, the carrying out of a reasonable job search and the reporting the results to the commission." This was never done by the commission. Then on page 26 we read that if circumstances warrant-
-the claimant is to be contacted by the insurance agent and counselled either in person, by telephone or letter, on his or her responsibilities in maintaining eligibility for benefits. In addition, the agent should determine when a claimant's change in status occurred and make the necessary revision to the claim.
That was never done. Then it says:
A disentitlement should not be imposed... if investigation reveals that a claimant was ignorant of the requirement to conduct an active search for work, or misunderstood the procedure.
I submit it is obvious that Mrs. Hirsch did not understand the procedures because the procedures were never explained to her. I wish the minister or the chairman of the Unemployment

Insurance Commission would explain to me how a claimant is supposed to understand and follow the procedures if the real meaning of those procedures is either inadvertently or deliberately kept from him. I say the result of this procedure is that the commission has been able to cut off thousands of people from benefit-a disgraceful situation. On pages 27 and 28 of this document they say:
The number of contacts made with employers and employment agencies or the manner in which these contacts are made cannot be enunciated in a general policy directive. Both quantity and quality of contacts must be determined by the number of potential job opportunities in the community within the claimant's occupation, the number of employers, the length of time a claimant has been employed and the manner in which unemployed persons with the claimant's occupation would customarily find re-employment. The assessment of a reasonable and customary search for work is therefore a matter of judgment on the part of the adjudicator.
Mr. Speaker, of course they cannot enunciate these things in a general policy directive, especially if they wish to use it as a device for cutting off people. I submit it would take a lawyer to understand all the ramifications of that paragraph. I suggest the wording of that clause is not the result of inadvertence- that the clause is there precisely to give the commission, on the advice of the government, the opportunity to cut off people. That, again, is a disgraceful situation.
Anyway, despite the fact that there is nothing in the record to show that I intervened on Mrs. Hirsch's behalf, her case was reheard. But it was a hearing by the same board, bound by the same jungle of laws and regulations, bound by the same prejudices-and I say this advisedly; I know at least two members of the board. And despite the fact that Mrs. Hirsch indicated clearly the whole range of job applications she had made, not just in the field of social work but in the field of personnel and other work, her application was turned down. I might say that Mrs. Hirsch did apply for work as a clerk at Eaton's. She was told that she was overqualified. The application form required her to list her previous experience, and she whas then told by Eaton's that she was overqualified. Yet the board referred to this in a way which would seem to indicate that it was her fault she was overqualified. So despite my intervention, Mrs. Hirsch lost her case.
However, 1 have been pressing the department pretty hard, and after a number of other communications I received a letter, addressed to me from the commission, dated July 14, 1977. It stated in part:
I would like to advise you of specific developments that will, 1 believe, go a long way to resolving the problem you have noted to my attention.
A second appeal to a board of referees on Mrs. Hirsch's case was held on June 29 and again the board ruled unanimously that the decision to deny her benefits was proper. It is my understanding that your office was advised before the hearing in order for you or another representative to attend. As a result of this second hearing it must be concluded that appeal action on this case has been essentially exhausted.
I would also like to advise, however, that we are in the process of developing refinements to the existing interview and active job search programs that will provide more specific information to claimants required to search for work. It is our intent to include on the active job search form a portion to be completed by the insurance agent showing the occupation(s) in which the search should be carried out together with the type and number of contacts that should be made. Specific indications of the need for an expanded job search will be shown and
July 19, 1977

discussed with the claimant as part of the interview program. These changes should be effected within the next few months.
If the commission does what Mr. Tuck has indicated in his letter, people will be told in future what kind of work they will have to look for if they are to continue to get unemployment insurance benefits. But it does not help Mrs. Hirsch. Why did this happen? When I spoke to the labour member on the board of referees-he is a good chap and I know he is concerned about people-he said, "We do not have the authority to do what you suggest, because the act is written in a certain way".
I said, "There is nothing in the act to prevent you". He said, "The regulations are written that way". I asked to see them, because I thought he was misinformed. I went to Mr. Tuck, and Mr. Tuck said, "It could not have happened. All my officers know they have to tell the people these things." Well, there is not a tittle of evidence that the benefit control officer said to Mrs. Hirsch, "This is what you have to do."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the amendment which has been proposed by my hon. friend from Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), namely, that this bill be hoisted for six months and be reconsidered at that time, is a very wise one. Since we last discussed this measure a couple of weeks ago I have received further correspondence from across the country. I should like to put some of it on the record. The first is a telegram from the International Woodworkers of America, the Canadian Labour Congress affiliate, local 1-118. A copy of the telegram was sent to every member of the Liberal caucus. The gist of the telegram is as follows:
The membership of local 1-118, IWA Victoria, are protesting very strongly the enactment of Bill C-27 and particularly those parts that will have the effect of creating unnecessary hardships on those people unemployed and those who will become unemployed. As we are sure you are aware of the unemployment and lack of employment in this area, we feel sure you must be aware of the extreme hardship this bill will create on your constituents. Please reply.
That telegram was signed by Murray Drew, business agent. I received a letter from a Parti Quebecois member of the Quebec national assembly, Mr. Gerard Gosselin, the deputy for Sherbrooke. He wrote to me as follows:

Mr. Rodriguez,
Allow a member of the Quebec National Assembly to congratulate you on your most relevant comments on the effects of Bill C-27 on the Canadian unemployed.
I am deeply concerned about the matter and according to my estimates, over 60,000 Quebec jobless will thus be stricken from the unemployment insurance rolls in Canada. This is an abominable transfer of the responsibility for supporting the unemployed from the federal to the provincial government, thus increasing considerably the costs of social welfare in Quebec, even though the federal government is still trying to deceive us about the effects of its legislation on the provincial welfare schemes. For your information, sir, please note that the Quebec social welfare scheme is already supporting 98,600 people who are deemed employable. Because of the new federal policies, this number of recipients will probably increase by some tens of thousands.
The present Ottawa administration assumes unfairly its responsibilities for Fighting unemployment and supporting the unemployed; even though the ben-
Employment and Immigration
efits paid by Ottawa to Quebec jobless are rather substantial, it is a fact that the high rate of unemployment in this province is the direct result of the broad economic policies of the central government which have disastrous consequences on our economy: for instance, its tariff policies on Quebec textiles, footwear, clothing and agricultural industries; its oil (the Borden Line), automobile, transportation, purchasing and capital investment policies.
The broad economic policies of the central government are the cause of unemployment in Quebec and of the ever decreasing number of jobs in the sensitive area of secondary industries.
Sir, I should appreciate very much being advised of the gist of the remarks you have made in the House on Bill C-27, as well as of any relevant material against this legislation.
1 am much concerned about the implications of this bill, and I intend, together with a number of my colleagues, to denounce it.
Thanking you in advance for your co-operation, sir, I remain.
Yours truly,

I have touched on the questions raised by the Premier of New Brunswick respecting the lack of any meaningful consultation between the federal government and provincial government. Premier Hatfield has accused the federal government of conducting a monologue rather than a dialogue. As I pointed out, the premier indicated this was an ad hoc response to what is a grave concern, rather than a long term plan to create employment opportunities in Atlantic Canada.
We in the House know that when the government first brought in this bill it moved the minimum attachment period to the work force from eight weeks to 12 weeks. It was only because of the fear of embarrassment on the part of the government that its backbenchers would vote against it and embarrass the devil out of the government that it brought in the compromise solution which is now in the bill. Once again the Liberal party has shown that it is prepared to compromise its principles; it could not even hold to the principle it established in the bill originally.

speechtext: Typical.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, it is very typical. The premier of New Brunswick also pointed out the difficulties he is having in regard to regional rates of unemployment. He expressed concern not only about the minimum attachment period and the length of benefits, but also about job sharing and the so-called creative use or developmental use of unemployment insurance funds.
The other surprising and most disappointing thing about this debate on Bill C-27 so far has been the performance in the House of the official opposition. By its silence, the Conservative party has acquiesced to this measure. It has broken faith with the unemployed in regions of the country where unemployment has unfortunately become a way of life. Not one voice in the Conservative opposition has been raised in the discussion of this bill, even though it has been at third reading stage for the last three to four weeks. A Conservative premier even took the time to write me a brief respecting the amended bill. But when the votes come on the amendments at third reading stage, members of the official opposition run for cover. They sit in their seats until the votes come; they then run behind the curtains. That is most regrettable and shameful.

July 19, 1977
Employment and Immigration
As for the reasons for wanting to give this bill a six months' hoist, I can reiterate old arguments and add new ones. We have already said that the bill is based on a false premise. It is based on a document known as the comprehensive review. The last time I spoke on this bill I pointed out several inaccuracies in the review. In many instances outdated statistics were used. In addition, they were far too narrow. For example, in section B the review states the Canadian labour force is characterized by a high degree of mobility. To support that statement they use job separations for one year only, 1974, and use address changes in 1970 and 1971. That is garbage, Mr. Speaker. It is absolutely useless in making a meaningful decision on unemployment insurance. It indicates that high wage increases have exceeded productivity increases. They have used only one year, 1974, and have made a comparison between Canadian and United States increases, which are not comparable in the first place. Thus, it is completely useless and inaccurate.
Approximately a week ago the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) made reference in his speech to the automotive industry. He showed conclusively that Canadian workers are far more productive than their American counterparts. Yet we pay more for the same automobile selling in the United States made by Canadian workers. In the comprehensive review, which was criticized and on which this bill is based, there is a statement that was arrived at by the UIC people. It refers to the fact that males with eight to 11 insured weeks in both years have a higher rate of disqualification than those with 12 or more insured weeks. On the other hand, females with 12 or more weeks have a higher incidence of disqualification and disentitlement than those with eight to 11 insured weeks.
On May 28, 1975, the former minister of manpower and immigration, in the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, said the following:
The incidence of disentitlement or disqualification, as an effect of failure to meet one's obligation under the act, is lower amongst the group with a minor attachment to the work force-
Again, we have printed information which has no relevancy to the bill we are dealing with. The entire bill is based on this comprehensive review which is not worth the paper it is written on. Members of parliament were asked to debate a bill which was based on inaccurate information.

Hon. members opposite can sit there yelling and screaming, but they never get up to make meaningful speeches. This bill was also based on an in-house report which contained a section devoted to the employment patterns in the Atlantic provinces. I have dealt with that section at some length before, but I should like to point out some of the things that were said about Canadian people, particularly those in Newfoundland where the latest rate of unemployment is over 13 per cent.

The report indicated that there was an indication some employers in smaller isolated communities deliberately hire seasonal workers in such a way as to provide at least a minimum number of insured weeks to as many persons as possible, thereby ensuring an adequate work force at their doorstep when needed. This report was prepared by the people of UIC, obviously to rationalize a piece of legislation to be stuck in front of this minister's nose. The minister was told to legislate, and like a monkey on a string he acts out the power trips of the bureaucracy, as the Liberals sit and dream of ways to move each other up the ladder, to lift the ceilings on executive salaries in the public service and give themselves raises.
These salaries are now at a point where they are going past $60,000. What does this minister, elected by the people of Canada to make decisions, do? "How high do I jump", is what he says. That is not what we expected from the minister. He should lay down a policy in this country and not be subject to their policy-making. It is a complete reversal. The employment patterns in the Atlantic provinces, as referred to in the report, indicate that the seasonal inshore fishermen may have some difficulty operating for ten weeks in the Stephensville area. It has been said in committee by the bureaucrats that there is no reason in the world why the people of Atlantic Canada cannot get eight weeks of work. The employment patterns in the Atlantic regions have no relevance to this bill.

The hon. members for Quebec ought to listen. There were polls conducted by the Toronto Star and Le Devoir regarding the referendum in Quebec. It is interesting to note that in both those polls the people placed a great deal of emphasis on the

economic health of their provinces and a great deal of emphasis on employment. This government thinks it has the national issue all locked up. They are missing the boat. Every time employment goes up a percentage point, Mr. Levesque indicates that he has a federal yoke around his neck which he has to get rid of. He also indicates that there is nothing he can do about the economic situation in Quebec. "It is those maudits federalists, let us get rid of them and then I can do something". That is their game. Mr. Levesque is gaining from the fumbling and bumbling and lack of economic policies by the federal government. Lo and behold, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) runs around the country benefiting from everything that has any connection with a poll which shows the separatists are gaining ground. The Prime Minister says to the Anglophones, "I will save the country; I will unite it." The Liberal party members have been wearing their great big buttons. That is the greatest threat to unity in this country-the Liberal party.

speechtext: There they sit, an alliance for power. We have seen the defections. We have seen how they are prepared to compromise their principles. Indeed, the other day somebody said that the Liberal Party of Canada was like a whore- it will take anyone.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
What are the solutions? Have they put forward anything at all with respect to employment opportunities in this country? What do I read in "Integration"? Obviously, the bureaucrats have already passed the bill themselves. They have put out a new document called "Integration". It is a document put out by the Department of Manpower and Immigration. It quotes the deputy minister's view on what full employment is from the point of view of the government. This is what Mr. Manion says:
"We are aiming at a full employment policy through these public programs coupled with developmental funds," added Mr. Manion. "Our employment strategy is designed to reduce the impact of unemployment and maximize employment opportunities".
The deputy minister is proposing that the job sharing programs and the developmental uses of UIC are the government's approach to full employment in Canada. It is rather interesting to see another article in the same paper, "Integration", written by a young woman who has never worked in her life. After graduation she went down to the Manpower office to look for work. They have a new system there now. They feed information into a computer which then tells them what are the job inclinations of the person applying for a job. The young woman who wrote the article is named Heather Hand, and the article is entitled, "Talk to the computer". Do you know what the computer spewed out that that young woman,
Employment and Immigration
who has never worked in her life before, is qualified to do? This is what she wrote;
I couldn't stand the suspense-
As she waited for the computer to give the answers.
-so I asked what they were:
3330-110 Producer, motion picture 3330-118 Producer, broadcasting 3330-150 Director, motion picture 3330-158 Director, broadcasting
That is what the machine said the young woman is qualified to do. That is the approach of matching people to jobs and full employment. Manpower offices now have computers, and computers are supposed to find jobs for people. It is marvellous! I think we had better disintegrate "Integration". The other provision that we oppose in the bill concerns the developmental uses of the unemployment insurance fund. We are opposed to this sort of thing. In effect, the government could use the unemployment insurance fund to give supplementary payments to those involved in a job sharing situation. It proposes, also, that the unemployment insurance fund be used for training people. All of us can subscribe to the theory that people should be trained, either on the job or anywhere else. Surely if the government wants to do that, then it should take the money out of the general revenues of the government so that the taxpayers can see that this much money is going to training and this much money is going to unemployment insurance.
We say that you cannot prostitute the unemployment insurance fund by using the fund to do other things than what it is supposed to do. Indeed, as an employee group which came before the committee said, they were completely opposed to job sharing and had grave doubts about the training programs which were proposed. The minister, with all his bureaucrats, proudly stood up in the committee and said that they had an advisory committee which gives them advice, and they welcomed the advice. The advisory committee reported in the annual report of 1976, and this is what they had to say about developmental uses of unemployment insurance:
A further meeting was held in December, 1976, for the specific purpose of reviewing the developmental uses of unemployment insurance in the areas of job creation and work sharing. The committee expressed very serious reservations about these approaches, particularly as they do not, in the committee's view, represent an appropriate use of the unemployment insurance program.
The committee feels very strongly that the minister should give careful thought to these views, which are unanimously shared by members of the committee.
He has received advice from the advisory committee to the Unemployment Insurance Commission, and he has received advice and evidence in committee from employer and employee groups. He has received it from the opposition parties in committee before the Conservatives lost their tongues. All the advice said: No, we should not use the fund for developmental uses of unemployment insurance. There is no point in having an advisory committee if its advice is thrown aside or ignored completely.
We have grave doubts about the whole thrust of the length of benefit period. As you know, in this bill the government, as

July 19, 1977
Employment and Immigration
a sop to the backbenchers in the Liberal party, proposed the imposition of 54 unemployment regions. Those of us who deal with the unemployment insurance fund every day of our lives as members of parliament know how complicated it is. The unemployment rate in each of these 54 regions will determine the minor attachment period and the length of the benefit period. I gave some examples of how it would work. If a person who lives in Nova Scotia, where the unemployment rate is approximately 13.2 per cent or more, works ten weeks, that person would get unemployment insurance benefits for 42 weeks. If a person who lives in the lower mainland of Vancouver, where the unemployment rate is 8.5 per cent, works ten weeks, that person would get no benefits. I suggest to you that 8.5 per cent is above the national unemployment rate in this country and it should not matter where you live in the country. If you are unemployed in Toronto, in Newfoundland or in Vancouver, you are unemployed, and the effects of unemployment on the lives of our people, regardless of region, are equally bad. It is just as debilitating to be unemployed in the east as it is in the west, north or south. In no way could this party support the discriminatory legislation this government is proposing in Bill C-27.
Another concern we have expressed time and again has to do with where unemployment hits hardest. We have said the important issue at the moment is unemployment opportunities. We have asked questions day after day in this House. We identified this issue months ago. We have made specific suggestions about creating short-term employment opportunities as well as long-term employment opportunities.
This government is a typical Liberal government which recognizes shifts in the wind. It can accept the biggest fascist in Canada into its ranks. I suppose it could also accept any well known leftist. It can absorb anyone, and I referred to an analogy earlier. In this particular instance, the Liberal Party has perceived that there is a move to the right in Canada, and it is tightening-up things like unemployment insurance to show the Canadian people how tough it is. It is easy to be tough with the unemployed, especially when they are young. Those who can find work are laid off very quickly, or they move from one job to another because of the present state of our economy.
A growing number of women are heads of households. They are no longer so-called working wives, a situation which the minister would have us believe is a luxury. Women with children are contributing in a meaningful way to the support of their families. We can no longer dismiss them. I can think of no better way to describe the problem than the way in which the leader of my party described it. He described it as follows:
Is it any wonder the Parti Quebecois has such strong support from young Quebeckers when one in every five persons under 24 is without work in that province and when half of the new unemployment in Canada in the past two years has occurred in Quebec?
The duty of an effective national government of whatever stripe is to govern in such a way as to see that its citizens can lead useful and productive lives. The Trudeau government has failed to meet this responsibility in nine years of office-
I recall 1968 when the swinging Prime Minister was diving off springboards. He never made any promises. Everybody said, "Isn't it wonderful; for a change, a politician who doesn't make a promise?" However, I remember two things the Prime Minister said during that 1968 campaign because I was very actively working at that time for our party's representative in Nickel Belt. The Prime Minister said that while he would not make any promises, he would work at two things. He said he would try to eliminate regional disparities in this country, and that he would work to bring about national unity. Here we are, nine years later. Is the country any more united than it was nine years ago?

speechtext: No wonder the Prime Minister does not want to talk about them.

speechtext:
He does not want to talk about them. The Liberal party has the ability to shift its position to accommodate whatever it thinks is in the wind. We, in this party, have said to the government time and again that we need short-term approaches as well as long-term policies which would set the base for employment as the work force grows. The government made a great big hullabaloo about the most recent budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). That hullabaloo was echoed in the province of Ontario over the budget which was brought down a few weeks later by that darling of the Chamber of Commerce, Darcy McKeough. That budget was a carbon copy of the budget brought down by the federal Minister of Finance. The federal Minister of Finance accepted the fact that full employment nationally is going to be anywhere upwards of 8 per cent. Tweedledee in the province of Ontario said we must live with 5.3 per cent in Ontario.
In its budget the federal government said that we still must depend on the private sector to create employment, and it gave out all kinds of hand-outs to the private sector. It handed out tax concessions when there are already too many tax concessions, in spite of the fact that we are operating at only 82 per cent of plant capacity. The chickens are coming home to roost. In a recent statement a chap by the name of Hugh Stevens, president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association-

Sinclair's brother?

July 19, 1977

speechtext:
They could be related. They are in the same field, banking. In a statement, he said he shared the concern of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) about unemployment, but he said that manufacturers cannot invest to create new jobs until the idle plant and equipment they already have is more fully used. That is why members of my party criticized the budget of the Minister of Finance. We asked why he was priming the pump when the pump was not being fully utilized. We asked why he was giving tax concessions for plant expansion when plant capacity was operating at only 82 per cent. Mr. Stevens went on to say:
Investment can only be made when the economics justify it. The fact is that much of Canadian manufacturing is in an extremely precarious position as a result of the excessive increases in Canadian costs in recent years, including wages, fringes, taxes, construction costs and interest rates.
The article which quotes Mr. Stevens also notes that perhaps the major factor dampening business expansion plans is the low operating rate of existing plant and equipment. Mr. Stevens observed that the average capacity utilization rate in manufacturing is stagnant at about 82 per cent. We have said that the government should not prime the pump at the top; that should be done down at the low income levels. We have also said that we should not go on developing the economy of Canada as a hinterland. We cannot go on shipping out raw materials. We cannot go on shipping out jobs with those raw materials. Many Liberals who sit on the back benches come from the hinterland parts of their provinces. Many hon. members from the Atlantic region come from the hinterland of the economy because their constituents take raw materials out of the ground. They fish for raw material. They cut raw materials down. We keep shipping out raw materials, and along with them go jobs.
We have said that we need policies geared to economic planning. We have said that if we are going to mine in Canada, the products we mine should be finished to a final product here. Not only do we encourage outsiders to take our resources but we even pay them to depreciate our resources. In the province of Ontario there are depreciation allowances, and we pay mining companies to depreciate our raw materials. We need long-term policies.

by the party in power. I deplore such an attitude. Yet, the fact remains that this attitude permeates all their actions. They claim to have the right to say everything and deny it to others who could point out their errors. More often than otherwise they just fool around. Even now, they do not have the decency to rise and speak on as important a topic as Bill C-27. We hear them shout, joke, show off, as we say in French "peter de la broue", but they do not have the decency to rise in the House as the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Bussieres)-

speechtext: He did not speak at all, he is incapable of it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
-to rise in the House and discuss those topics their electors would have them bring up. There are more than enough unemployed in the riding of Compton, just as there are in that of the hon. member who was shouting a moment ago. They did not have the decency to take into consideration the remarks made by their electors.
Yet those people sent in lists of names, they signed petitions to point out to the government and its members their disappointment, their disenchantement with Bill C-27. We are now discussing at the third reading stage a motion to stand Bill C-27 for six months, so that government members can read their mail and bring the corrections that are needed to this piece of legislation that is a disaster for the working population in Canada. The intent with this bill is to put the blame on the worker. If he cannot find work, if for some reason he finds it difficult to keep a job, he is accused by the government of abusing the system, so they want to make it more restrictive. The government, however, find no way that would allow the worker to find acceptable employment on a steady, yearly basis.
But they found the way to penalize him by increasing to 12 weeks the eligibility period. This is hurting those who find it hard to keep a job. We often receive letters from employers who make the personal effort of keeping an employee on the job one or two weeks more than the six or seven weeks they would normally employ them. Small businessmen make that effort so that the workers involved at least make up in unemployment insurance benefits for the little time they could spend at work. Such an effort the government do not make. They put forward the bill to reduce workers to the bare minimum, and they put the blame on the individual. And indirectly, especially in the province of Quebec, when they disentitle the greater number of unemployed, they know that automatically they will depend on welfare, so that the blame will be on the big bad government that was elected on November 15.
Well, Mr. Speaker, we know that this problem has been with us much longer than that. With an 8, 10, 12 week period there is disparity. It was said earlier that the government is committed to eliminating regional disparities, but it is quite the opposite. They are creating 54 disparities, 54 regions where they will be playing with 8, 10 and 12 week periods. They are going to play with that and another department of the government will say to the workers: now, we are going to
7798

July 19, 1977
Employment and Immigration
move you to another area. 1 can hardly wait to see the problems those people are going to be faced with when they move from an eight-week area to a twelve-week area. 1 can hardly wait to see their faces when they argue with the officials. They tell them nothing about that. Indeed not, they hold a knife against their throat and tell them: Well, that is your problem. Does the bill talk about employment insurability? Not at all.
We have stacks of cases, discussions, and the UIC is now taking refuge behind the taxation department and tells people: Well, your job is not insurable, you are not entitled to unemployment insurance, you do not even have the right to contribute to unemployment insurance, you do not even have the right to pay unemployment insurance in order to draw benefits when you lose your job. I know of specific cases where a storekeeper hires one of his children-he does not have the right. If he hires his neighbour's son and sends his own son to work for the neighbour, then after such an exchange the employment is insurable. But under the regulations, if he wants to hire his own son, the latter is not insurable, he does not have the right to pay unemployment insurance premiums on a seasonal basis.
I am talking about a tourist area-Temiscamingue-where during the summer there are what are known as outfitters, people who work for a specific period, from May to September, who need a job for eight, seven, six or ten weeks, it depends, people who look after the tourists who come to those areas. If one hires his son, the son will not be entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. If he hires the neighbour's son, then it is all right, he is entitled to unemployment insurance. That is the rule of the game. The government, through all kinds of means, through bills such as Bill C-27, has created situations where individuals are forced to be as crooked as the government to get what is due to them.
They are forced to cheat with the officers and search for reasons.
We know of a case now in the province of Quebec where the provincial government, through its highways department, is hiring people in the riding of Temiscamingue for only eight weeks. Then they are laid off, after eight weeks only, and another group of 75 people is hired for another eight week period. If that is not a fight between two government levels, I wonder what it is with the crazy regulations we now have. What change will be brought into it? The federal government says: No, we will block the unemployed and passed the buck to the provincial government through welfare. The provincial government answers: No, we will never accept that. Let those people take their responsibilities. Yet, those people are laid off after eight weeks of work.
It is a game of political confrontation instead of an administration that assists people. A further point: there is no change in sections 172 and 173 concerning leave credits and terms of employment. Nothing at all! They took advantage of that again last week, when we had to go before the board of referees and plead cases successfully before three judges who

ruled unanimously in favour of the recipient. However, the next day, the board informed us that the case will be referred to the umpire. The three judges of the board of referees appointed by the government cannot even make a unanimous decision. But it is an never-ending game where they always lay the blame on the individual instead of trying to find a solution.
We are told that the government is trying to assist small businesses so that they may create work and produce more. Canadian productivity is increasing, but we know that it is gradually increasing through automation which undeniably causes unemployment. But the government is there precisely to deal with the affairs of the country, to be able to give. The number of jobs is reduced but the government is there precisely to establish policies which would ensure the individual the necessary purchasing power to buy the production of the machine. Unfortunately, the government lacks the decency to think this way. It tries to put the blame on the individual. When in trouble, it says that the situation depends on other countries, that if we have inflation in Canada, it is because of some other countries.
As far as inflation is concerned, prices increase and companies have to spend more to obtain the supplies they need to manufacture. Therefore some companies close down. And if the workers are unemployed, it is their fault; they are lazy because they worked only from eight to ten weeks, depending on the area, or perhaps for twelve weeks. The blame is always put on the individual. Bill C-27 should be entitled "Import controls" rather than deal with unemployment insurance. If, at the very outset, something had been done to deal with the problems of importation into Canada, there is no question that this would have promoted employment. In the Eastern Townships, textile plants are going out of business; furniture manufacturers have gone bankrupt, five of them, one after the other, in Victoriaville. The shoe manufacturers are also going bankrupt. They are all closing down because of the free flow of imports! And then, people will say: "We have too many unemployed"! If we have too many unemployed, something has to be done to reduce their number, and to this end, a bill is introduced, Bill C-27, intended to reduce the number of unemployed.
But what has been done to create jobs for these people? Absolutely nothing. This amounts to putting band aids on wooden legs. There are all kinds of excuses, investing in a given field, to create four, five or six jobs, while at the same time 50 or 60 jobs are destroyed in the same area. There is such a case in my own riding at the present time. We have to fight with various departments in order to get the grants needed to help small businesses. We have to appeal to both the provincial government and the federal government for investments in a region where there is about 22 to 24 per cent of unemployed. But, when we meet them in the streets, or try and count them, we are more likely to find 30 per cent than 24 or 22 per cent.
But the government allows this situation when it refuses to help small businesses, as was the case recently with Quebec Iron Foundries, in Noranda. There was an agreement between
July 19, 1977

the Department of Manpower and Immigration and the company to retrain the employees in other fields. They are not guaranteed a job, they are retrained in a field other than the foundry, which served the Noranda mine. There was no thought given to retraining the company. It gets benefits from something else to guarantee jobs to the employees. But the blame is placed on the employees. The company closes down and the employees are dismissed. After that, they are told: "Very well, we shall retrain you." But in what field? Where? How? Why? No one knows. But they will be retrained. Afterwards, if they have not found a job, on the basis of Bill C-27 they will be told: "Well, my friend, you will have to get busy. You will have to look for a job, everywhere, like the unemployed are now doing." They are looking for jobs. They are now being told that they have not searched for employment in their area. They have looked only in their municipality, yes, in their municipality. You can ask the officials and the minister: "What is the municipality? What does it mean?" The previous speaker spoke about Winnipeg. If I live at one end of Winnipeg, I can tell you that it is quite a long way to go to work at the other end. The problem is the same in Montreal. If I live in Pointe-aux-Trembles and if 1 have to go to work in Dorval, this poses a transportation problem. But no consideration is given to that. The unemployed has not looked for a job; he restricted his search to his municipality.
In rural constituencies like my own where the next town is 40, 50 or 60 miles away, where there is no public transport, where the unemployed has been looking for a job in his town or the neighboring town, with a population of perhaps four or five thousand people, it is impossible to find a job. He is still cut off from the unemployment benefits because he has not looked in his area. When we try to find out how many miles does the area cover and what services are given, it is impossible to find out. The unemployment officials do not know what is an area. That person is on the unemployment roll, he has no car, no public transportation. How could he go 40 or 45 miles away, twice a day, to find a job? And people are denied unemployment insurance benefits on grounds such as these!
The bill refers to 54 districts. Employment opportunities, means of transportation to and from work and the total number of unemployed should at least be considered in these 54 districts! 1 suppose there is some assessment, to a certain extent but these things are not being considered. They apply the same scale to a region or a large urban centre, no matter what employment opportunities there are in a given area. They do not take those factors into account. For the same reasons, these people are denied unemployment insurance benefits and in addition, the onus is on the worker. He must prove he has been actively seeking employment. The applicant goes to the federal manpower centre, to the provincial manpower office and comes back home because they have nothing to offer him. He contacts the four or five industries where he used to work. They have nothing for him either. After a while those workers have to accept any job that is offered to them. What will Bill C-27 do to give workers adequate protection against officious
Employment and Immigration
civil servants? Nothing at all. All they try to do is to put the burden on the worker's shoulders.
What should our position be on this? When workers are displaced by machines, are they entitled to make a living or not? When, for economic reasons, whether from within or without the country, such sclerosis, and unemployment is created, resulting in financial disaster for' the people concerned, are the jobless not entitled to a living? That is the whole question we must ask ourselves. If it is admitted they have a right to a decent living, well, legislation should provide a decent living for them. No bill like C-27 should be tolerated, the impact of which is to back the unemployed into a corner and gag and belittle them or force them on welfare, and then, once they are there, make it even worse for them, by making them crawl to officials for a mere pittance. That is why, for years now, the Social Credit Party of Canada has advocated and still does a guaranteed annual income for everybody, so that if someone loses his job, he will at least be assured a sufficient amount to live on. And he will be entitled and allowed to look for another job, and when he has found it, this guaranteed annual income will be a supplement to his income. It will not be a penalty as it is now.
If someone collecting unemployment insurance does a little work in a week, he is penalized and his benefits are reduced. If he works for more than four weeks, then he is "cancelled", out! He cannot get benefits for four weeks then this clause is used and he is kicked out, he is no longer eligible. He is not entitled to unemployment insurance benefits anymore. We have at least cancelled that one a little bit but only to find some other devious way, a little better than bear traps this time. Not mouse traps, bear traps this time.
That is why we support this motion to put this bill off for six months; if it were possible to put it off for two years, we would do it, because it does not solve the problem. It does not help to improve some situations. This bill creates a situation which is worse than the one existing before. It brings a small improvement on one side and a big failure on the other. A small correction is made on the right for an even bigger failure on the left. It is a continuous game. So, we oppose that bill, and we support the motion to put it off for six months, because in our opinion, many people have representations to make, there will be many petitions drawn by people who were caught in the unemployment problem, people who had to live with it. These are not businessmen.
I had a conversation with a member of the government who met businessmen in his riding; they told him: "That is a good bill". That man has never been on unemployment insurance in his life. He does not know what it is and he even added: I do not know what it is. I have never been on unemployment. But eight weeks is too short. Twelve weeks, you should put a longer period. Such is the advice given to some government members. They should have seen those who are on unemployment insurance, those who have to rely on unemployment benefits for some part of the year to be able to eat during 52 weeks. They
80020-29'/2

July 19, 1977
Adjournment Motion
should have consulted those people before introducing a bill such as Bill C-27, and maybe we would not have such a long debate. Chances are the government would have come up with a legislation likely to solve the problem instead of creating one as it is the case now.
Those are the general comments I wanted to make. Mr. Speaker, we are going to continue to make such comments, such representations in the House of Commons as well as outside the House, because we know that most Canadians do not want a discriminatory measure but legislation which will allow them to live decently in this country. If we do not have enough jobs to go around we should at least give them an opportunity to rely on some sort of guaranteed income. It should not be an everlasting fight between men who seek the right to live and civil servants who always wonder whether the unemployed or the person without a job is entitled to the payment he needs to survive. Those are the comments I wanted to submit to the attention of the House and I hope hon. members will vote for that six month delay to allow the civil servants to read their correspondence and become conscious of the problem this bill will create for simple workers.
