subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said a while ago, I do not think that I have taken too much of the time of the House in connection with this bill and this afternoon I wish to support the motion introduced by the member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) suggesting to the government a six months's hoist in the consideration of this bill. Actually, Mr. Speaker, we would have many subject matters to deal with. And the reason we want that bill sent to the committee for six months to undergo a further study, is that we want, for example, a review of clause 29 which deals with the insured's qualification, of clause 38 which deals with sickness or pregnancy, of clause 27 which deals with the much talked about insurability, and of clause 31 which extends the qualifying period.
We also wish to discuss the board of referees, the immense power wielded by this body, the issue of the search for work and above all those explanations which the civil servants would have to give to the claimants. Finally, we want to study the issues raised by strikes, by vegetable and fruit pickers, by voluntary designations and make it mandatory for the employer to send immediately the termination of employment form, and so on. These are only a few points which I just mention and we would like all these matters to be dealt with in depth. This is why we want that bill sent back to committee in six months for it to undergo a more thorough study.
Mr. Speaker, for instance I find that clause 29, asking a claimant to have at least from ten to fourteen weeks of prior insurable employment to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits, is a direct attack against the unemployed, because it gives credence to the allegation that they should be considered guilty for their being unemployed. This new clause of the bill proposed by the government is a direct attack against the most defenseless people among the working class, in the sense that the majority of workers who only qualify with a minimum number of insurable weeks of work are the aged and those who have a low level of instruction who generally keep their jobs a shorter time because the type of jobs that are available to them are often for a short period. Students, for instance, who do not intend to go on with their studies and who, as their first work experience have been hired for the summer season, will find
July 19, 1977

themselves without a right to these benefits according to the new clauses of the bill.
The eight-week requirement could quite easily be met by those families or individuals who worked as fruit, vegetable tobacco, tomato or cucumber pickers in the various parts of Canada or elsewhere, but 1 say it will be very difficult for them to get twelve or fourteen weeks of employment. In its proposal the government completely overlooks modern personnel requirements in the private, public and quasi-public sectors. Increasingly businesses require specialized workers for short periods of time only. Specialized people are hired for definite jobs of a short duration.
Through this provision increasing the qualifying period to eight, ten and even fourteen weeks, the government and its supporters leave the impression that most unemployed who qualified with a minimum period of eight weeks were hardcore unemployed. For instance, jobs are marginal in my riding. Our unemployment rate of 26 or 27 per cent is a clear indication that job-seekers must search for a long time to get one of the few jobs. It is obvious that with such a bill, such a provision and many others, the government is trying to make an insurance scheme profitable by eliminating the factors which are more risky. Social legislation such as this one should not be administered according to the same criteria as those governing private enterprise, even less so when the workers are the ones paying for this insurance.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the insured who pays the premium is entitled to the benefit of his insurance.
I have always considered that unemployment insurance was like any other insurance, like fire insurance or accident insurance: when your house burns down or when you have an accident, you have the right to claim benefit from your insurance company. But I think that is the major problem with the insurers: once you have paid the premium, there are indeed so many investigations of all kinds that in the end, even with a paid up insurance policy, you cannot get any benefits. Yet, when dealing with a commercial insurance company, let us say a fire insurance company, if one is not satisfied with the settlement, one may sue the company and the latter will have to pay. But when you are dealing with government agencies, it is useless to think of taking any legal action since it is so difficult to have officers transferred and they always have the last word. I say that those who deprive the unemployed of their rights are in my opinion outright criminals.
Mr. Speaker, such cases happen every day. A member's office is a good place to get to know of such things and I am sure that government members experience the very same problems. I feel that what is lacking in all this is a little light and a little more understanding. Some may say that 1 am overdoing it, that I am going too far. Yet, after my party leader spoke this afternoon and gave us an idea of what is going on among the people, I should like to call upon the media in order to substantiate our claims.

This is what I have been in the process of doing all the time. It is stated here: Five officials denounce UIC roll reductions. That is why I was telling you that we must refer the bill back to committee in order that it be fully looked into. Let us stop playing on words. We are doing nothing here in this House but playing on words. We are creating problems for everybody. Even officials, imagine, five officials denouncing the cuts made by the UIC. I know the minister is aware of the fact, because I discussed it with him. I would like this to be looked into. Apparently, the truth must now be told behind curtains, because one is kaput if one is seen. I realize that there are still honest civil servants. That is why I want to mention this fact because everything is blamed on the officials who have to cope with the act all year long.
In my riding, I meet some officials twice, three or four times a year and that is what they tell me. Why don't you try to have more specific legislation and stop bothering us with all these troubles. That is also what we must do. This new legislation is even worse. Do you realize that for disqualification alone, there will be 54 different regions, 54 different cases to be assessed. I would not like to be in these officials' shoes. To say what they want to say, they have to hide under a hood. According to them, the department is trying to strike off 33 per cent more people from the rolls. Their heads hidden under a black hood and without telling names, these five officials have given-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, here are the reasons why I think consideration of this bill should be deferred for six months. It is because we have heard evidence such as this asking us to give the bill a six months' hoist. We want a six months' hoist. Do you understand? You have listened to all other members who gave their reasons why this delay is necessary. Why are you trying to prevent me from telling the truth when I am stating my case? It seems we are trying to hide the truth from the public. And yet, this is the truth, what is written, what appeared in the papers. It has to be said.
There are more jobless but less people who collect benefit. Such is the effect of the bill before us. This is why we want to send it back to the committee. Here we say: Mr. Cullen will want some explanations. But how come there are more unemployed and fewer benefits are paid. But no wonder, with the kind of bill we have; and if this bill is not amended, if it is not reviewed, if it is not referred to a committee for consideration, we will still have more unemployed and fewer beneficiaries, and the responsibility for it all will fall on the provincial government, as said the hon. member who spoke before me. The federal government collects the taxes, collects the contributions and when it has had enough, it says to the provincial governments; Now, you take the rest.
And once again the provincial government will have to assist those unemployed through the social welfare. This is the impact of this bill; this is why, Mr. Speaker, we want to give the bill a six month hoist. As far as I am concerned, I would like to give it a six year hoist so that I would not hear about it any more, but the amendment provided for six months only, and we have to comply with it. But, if we should pass this bill tonight, it will not do any good. We are going to be worse off than before. I was telling you earlier that we now have 24 per cent. That is again in the newspaper Le Quotidien of the 23rd. And some think that we are going to keep quiet in the House, that we are not going to speak out. No, Mr. Speaker, they are wrong because we are going to speak out and to denounce, because what is coming makes no sense. This bill must at all costs be referred to committee for a further detailed study, so that the unemployed may have what they are entitled to.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that it is absolutely essential that the powers of the board of referees be restricted in the course of the further consideration. At present, the board of referees is all powerful and solves about every problem in its own way, unless that is changed in the course of the further consideration of this bill. I just had a case in my riding. I will not mention names but that was very obvious to me. So, in its report, the board of referees states: the fact remains that the board of referees has the right and privilege to interpret the power, the power to decide which statement it will accept, and also to rule on the admissibility of the evidence. Imagine! It goes on to say: It should be noted, however, that it is not up to the claimant to decide on his availability. Imagine! The claimant, under the present act, has no longer even the right to say whether he is available or not. It is up to the board of referees-officials-to decide: You are available, you are not available.
Such problems keep cropping up in our ridings. And what I do not understand is that such cases can be pleaded and when carried through, something finally comes out of it. But why did they not do it right away? Because the act quite simply, is not clear, it is too confused, and the officials are not wizards either. They do their best. Let us not forget, as I said earlier, that I am not trying to lay the blame on public servants.
Certain public servants want to make money out of unemployment insurance, but others are honest. I simply say that the legislation is too restrictive and not clear enough, and this is why we want a six month hoist to have the opportunity to say what we think about certain sections of the bill. I have something to say about insurability. Who determines insurability? There are many cases in my constituency, Mr. Speaker, of workers who had to contribute. I have seen such cases over a period of two and a half years. They were asked to contribute every week, and after two and a half years, they became unemployed. The Unemployment Insurance Commission told them: "Well, you were allowed to contribute, but you were not supposed to." The companies and the employers do not know what is going on.
The legislation does not clearly state when someone must contribute to unemployment insurance and is entitled to the benefits. Not only is the Unemployment Insurance office not authorized to tell those people that they are not entitled to benefits, but their case has to be referred to the Department of National Revenue since it is the one which decides if a worker is insurable or not. After two or three years, the worker is told that he has contributed for nothing. I know of such cases. I say this quite advisedly, Mr. Speaker. This is why a six months hoist would give us time to discuss this question of insurability.
It is essential to get the facts straight. I strongly object to the Department of National Revenue determining if someone can get unemployment insurance. There is a limit to the number of times departmental responsibility can change. I was talking about this with the officials of my area, in Alma, and they told me: "Listen, we do not have any influence, we must wait up to four months to know what the department will do." These poor people were saying: "We are like you, Mr. Gauthier, we have to wait." Is the government aware of the problem? There is a wall. I had to leave. I commuted between the office and the department because the civil servants could not communicate together. That is how they take the unemployed for a ride. What do you think happens to an unemployed man who can hardly sign his name and is facing such a problem? He will lose his unemployment insurance benefits. Those are real cases, Mr. Speaker, and for that reason we want to delay that study for six months so we could set the facts straight as we see them every day.
We have also the important issue of pregnancy or sickness. That is another trick: A guy gets sick and he needs a medical certificate. So I tell him: Send your doctor's certificate. Then he sends his certificate but they do not get it. I know workers who sent eight certificates within seven months but civil
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
July 19, 1977

servants never received those famous certificates. Now I have them photocopied and send a dozen at the first opportunity because civil servants seem to lose them too easily. What I am complaining about now, what I have always asked for in this House is that the medical certificate be the only argument allowing a sick person to get his or her benefits. I have discussed that with doctors in my area. The doctor brings in his findings but at the insurance office it is a civil servant who will weigh the diagnosis. The doctor says six weeks rest, but civil servants figure that two weeks is enough. That is wrong, they should respect the medical diagnosis.
This is very clear, and I have been urging this for a long time. But let us respect the diagnosis of the physician. The civil servant is there to dictate letters and he has never practised medicine and does not know beans about it. However, he is one who decides whether a person has the right to be on sick leave for two, three, four or five weeks. This is ridiculous! I have always asked for this, without success. The physicians ask for this too, they want their certificates to be respected.
When a person is operated on for appendicitis, he gets four weeks leave, and I had the opportunity to discuss this with one of these civil servants who confirmed this to me. There can be all kinds of complications with appendicitis, Mr. Speaker. Even if the physician says this is acute appendicitis, and the knows his patient's need, he knows whether the person needs to stop working for eight or ten weeks, the civil servants tells us that it is four weeks according to the law. This is ridiculous! I had to defend such cases. It seems funny to say, maybe some of you would not believe me, but I had to go and defend such cases.
I also believe that as long as the legislation will not say specifically that the physician's diagnosis should be followed, we will be in the wrong. It seems to me that the government is relying more on its officials than on the physician. I for one can tell you that I have more faith in the physician than in the local official. It is sad to say, but I have always defended causes like that. The same thing goes for strikes. I see that time is going fast, but I wanted to say a few words on this subject to note what we are supposed to do and consider in the next six months regarding this bill. It is the same thing for strikes. Of course, when an industry strikes its workers are not allowed to get unemployment benefits. But what about those who are not union members, why should they be treated in the same way as those who are members of the union?
Within six months, those cases will have to be studied in a very specific manner to determine who is entitled to unemployment insurance and who will be penalized because of strikes. It must be realized that when there is a strike, strikers are not 100 percent for the strike, especially when their type of employment is not entirely related to the work performed by the real strikers. I think that we are witnessing these problems day in and day out and that they will keep arising because of the bill before us, if tonight we do not decide, once and for all,
Employment and Immigration
to clarify this situation and send this bill back for six months for further study on this matter.
Mr. Speaker, as for the extension of the qualifying periods, 1 think that while reading the bill the minister did not even think of workers who are injured on the job. There must absolutely be a special extension of the qualifying period in order that such persons who have received accident compensation benefits for a month, two months or even three months and did not collect unemployment insurance, will be able as soon as they are back on the job market, and available for but unable to secure employment, to receive unemployment insurance benefits. I think that this is a very legitimate demand. I can understand or I would rather think that there was perhaps a mistake, but I also believe that if we do not take the necessary steps to try and correct the defects that we keep finding in the present bill, we will keep giving the unemployed the run around and make them wait indefinitely. Last week, somebody told me that he had been waiting to collect his unemployment insurance benefits for the past fourteen months.
He had waited 14 months for the results of the studies. He had received a letter saying his case was under review. Mr. Speaker, I believe we are serious enough in this House and sincere enough to see to it that this bill is not voted upon tonight but referred instead for a real study, and not to be discussed with civil servants. Not that I blame those who are here. They have never been out in the field. They have no idea what goes on out there. They write the laws but know nothing about what is going on. We, however, live the whole year round with the unemployed out in the field. I think it would do them good to have an hon. member in their midst from time to time, an hon. member who comes from those areas, but, no, we come third class. It is quite forbidden to consult us, to ask our advice. They are the ones who decide under what conditions such and such an unemployed will get benefits. And there again, if one has good friends, good connections, things won't be too had. But if, unfortunately, one has no friends, it is often difficult to solve the case.
Indeed, we do run into cases like that. Mr. Speaker, I do hope this bill will not pass third reading tonight and that the amendment of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) will be accepted. I am sure that many government members would like to see the amendments I mentioned a while ago improve the shortcomings of the bill, and the only way to do that, once again, is to defer the bill and vote for the motion of the hon. member for Timiskaming.

Mr. Speaker, one really has the impression that this is not a democratic Parliament. Our colleagues seem shocked to see us rise and express the views of our constituents. Our democracy will survive so long as our democratic parliamentary system will be respected. Otherwise our system will disappear and then everybody will

July 19, 1977
Employment and Immigration
wonder how it happened. Freedom of speech! What has become of it?
Mr. Speaker, I hope that you at least understand me and will accept that I make some remarks on Bill C-27 and also on the motion to give the bill a six months' hoist for further consideration. I remember a few years ago when a similar piece of legislation was passed by the Canadian Parliament, the unemployment insurance act. Well, this Parliament wanted to safeguard the rights of the workers who happened to be out of work after the last world war. Before that war, Mr. Speaker, there was a period of acute unemployment during the economic recession from 1929 to 1939. At that time, there was no legislation to ensure the Canadian workers minimum income if unemployed. We had nevertheless various work programs. We had subsequently the relief program.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with all due respect, but in order to say anything sensible on the amendment, I must deal with the bill. That is why I have to remind the hon. members of the history of our unemployment insurance legislation and I don't know of any rule that prevents me from telling the House that before the introduction of the present unemployment insurance act, other events took place. I consider that I respect the Standing Orders and the Chair precisely by recalling those previous situations which later led Parliament to adopt a law providing for the unemployed worker some benefits which have been called unemployment insurance benefits.
Mr. Speaker, in the course of my functions, I had to cooperate in many instances to complete forms for workers who happened to be unemployed, to help them take advantage of this law adopted by Parliament which provided they could receive unemployment insurance benefits. What Parliament wanted at that time was to guarantee them a minimum income so they would not have to get into debt when they were unemployed. And I think I must commend the lawmakers of that time who were concerned about protecting the economic situation of people who after the 1939-1945 war could eventually be unemployed.
Later the law was amended a few times, Mr. Speaker, as it was in 1971 and again in 1977. Now we are on Bill C-27 and an amendment motion has been proposed by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), a motion which would delay the adoption of this bill for six months. Is it because the bill has to beget something in six months' time? Definitely not. It is not a

period set aside for confinement but a period set aside for reasoning, for thinking, that will allow the law-makers, the minister and the officers time to study this legislation in greater depth, to make it more consistent with the actual needs of the workers, of those who could possibly be unemployed some day, not of their own will, but due to unusual economic circumstances.
So, Mr. Speaker, I think that since Bill C-27 was introduced in this House, there has been no reason for changing our opinion on it. Of course, I do not want to repeat the very serious comments voiced by my colleagues in the House of Commons, and especially by the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne) who is particularly qualified to speak on labour matters, on questions relating to unemployment insurance entitlement and contributions. I think, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Kamouraska has shown during the last 15 years, in the speeches he has made before Parliament, that he is a truly responsible member, that he is sincerely working in the interest of his constituents, and that he is at the same time making sure that Canada can guarantee the security of the workers of our country, the security of our disabled citizens, of our widows, of our orphans and of all those who are destitute, so they are in a position to meet their obligations.
Mr. Speaker, are opposition members alone in objecting to Bill C-27? 1 do not think so. If we reread the comments made in the House by government members, on the majority side, I will not say in power, because they are not, but on the government or the majority side, well I remember among others the comments of the hon. member for Madawaska-Vic-toria (Mr. Corbin) who clearly stated in the House that he objected to Bill C-27 on second reading. He assumed his responsibilities and said that the bill did not meet the needs of workers for which it was meant and did not encourage them to work and contribute to the growth and development of our country.
Mr. Speaker, further on, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) in a document which he tabled and in his comments before the committee said:
In amending the unemployment insurance system, we are obviously facing the following dilemma: ensure better income protection for the claimant while giving him an incentive to work.
I more than agree. We must have in this country a legislation which would encourage any able-bodied man to work, whether in his own interest, in the interest of his community, his province or his country. I fully agree, but we must take into account the economic situation in which we live. The minister added:
The 1971 amendments have obviously helped provide adequate income maintenance.
That is true. The benefits granted to the unemployed helped them meet the needs of their families, or in the case of single persons, prevented them from sinking into debt, for otherwise they would have been compelled to borrow and mortgage their future.
July 19, 1977

Up to that point, I think the minister is right. He went on:
As well, the experience of the past five years abviously threw light on the elements of the system which had bad consequences on the labour force.
And yet, Mr. Speaker, you were here when the bill to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act was introduced in 1971. Members on the government side were saying that this legislation was the best in the world, that it would provide workers with a stable income while encouraging them to go back to work and get the available jobs.
The minister goes on:
Not only the comprehensive study on the unemployment insurance system in Canada, but also a wide variety of studies made by other agencies and individuals have enabled us to recognize and identify its effects. The proposals contained in Bill C-27 are designed to improve the balance between the components of the system and I am convinced of their appropriateness.
Mr. Speaker, it is either of two things: In 1971, it was logical to give workers the possibility of claiming unemployment insurance benefits after having contributed to the fund for eight weeks, whereas in 1977 we confess in the face of the whole country that this was a disastrous mistake. Well, Mr. Speaker, if we confess that this was a disastrous mistake to give benefits after eight weeks of work attachment in 1971, I think I am entitled to question whether at the end of one year, or two years of having had to live with Bill C-27, we would not ask the same question for the second time: was it not a mistake to establish a qualifying period of 10, 12 or 14 weeks according to the unemployment in each area, as the minister says.
And I quote what he said:
First of all, we shall increase by 12 weeks the benefit period during the regional extended benefit phase. During this phase, recipients will therefore be entitled to benefits for a possible maximum of 32 weeks instead of 20.
Additional weeks of benefits would depend on the regional unemployment rate, which appears in Schedule B which is annexed to the copy of my speech.
These are remarks which he made in the House when he moved the second reading of this bill. Well, Mr. Speaker, statistics are something which I believe in, but I do not trust them 100 per cent, and because of our experience with votes earmarked for the Canada Works and Young Canada Works programs, I am most careful because statistics are not always up to date. When we consider the figures published by Statistics Canada concerning the number of unemployed recorded on its rolls, and then consider the real number of unemployed people in our own regions, there are serious discrepancies, and this procedure affects unfavourably the poorer regions in our country.
It is on the basis of these statistics that, according to Bill C-27, unemployment insurance benefit entitlement will hinge for those who are unemployed. There is something which I may know better than anybody in Canada, Mr. Speaker, and it is that there are many Canadians who really want to work and earn their own living, but who simply cannot, because of economic conditions which are beyond their control.
Second, a percentage of the population wants to work in order to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits and then live on them without working, thus taking advantage of all the
Employment and Immigration
benefits that our partnership, our life in society has to offer. But even then, a distinction must be made. I think it is a small number. And I remember during the recession I referred to a moment ago, many jobless were termed as lazy by the authorities of the day because they did not want to work, but when the war broke out and all able-bodied men were called upon to enlist, they no longer were lazy. Thousands of our young people were willing to enlist because it was the only way to earn a living.
From 1939 to 1945, thousands of Canadians were called upon to work in our factories here and there and it was then acknowledged that those people were not lazy but hard-working who only want to earn good pay, to earn a decent living. Mr. Speaker, we are now going through an extremely difficult period when the best qualified people cannot find a job. I get mail every day in this connection from young people, people of all trades who write to me, who telephone me to ask me if it would not be possible to help them find a job.
I signed earlier some fifty letters before coming to the House recommending people to the Quebec manpower centres in Quebec City, Levis and Montmagny, not to ask for unemployment insurance benefits but to ask the public servants in those manpower centres to help those people find a job. Mr. Speaker, how gratifying it is to be able to help someone find a job so that this person will have the pleasure of saying at the end of each day: I earned my daily bread. I have done something for my country and my country will benefit from it because my country has given me plenty. Mr. Speaker, when you reach age 24 or 30, and have scores of diplomas stuffed in your pockets, diplomas which have been paid for by your predecessors and which are very hard to get these days, because education has become terribly expensive, when we see these young people so healthy and so fully qualified, having acquired the great qualification of the day, the qualification to be unemployed, we wonder what this parliament has been doing to deal with such an unacceptable situation. But, except in wartime, the private sector alone is not in a position to provide jobs for all the qualified people in our country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the dinner recess I had still a few minutes left to finish my comments on the motion under consideration. I was explaining how Canadian industries are at present unable to create the necessary jobs to cope with the manpower needs in Canada. That is one of the reasons why we now have more than a million unemployed.

Such is modern democracy. A working permit. You are qualified, you were trained as a heavy equipment operator, but that is not enough. You must first obtain a working permit in order to get a job. That working permit is no easy thing to get, and God knows if I am not aware of that. So we make things more difficult. Secondly, there is not enough room available in those schools for training all the applicants. In my area alone, there are already 1200 names on the waiting list, people who want to retrain as heavy equipment operators. They have to wait for 6, 12, 18 or even 24 months before they can attend classes.
Mr. Speaker, I have here a list of employers operating in the James Bay area, just to show that there are employers really willing to help workers to get a job. There may be 150 firms. I did not count them. Anyway, I have seven or eight full pages. Some are operating in the North, on the Labrador side, and when someone asks me for help in finding a job, I send him the full list to show that there are employers. But do those employers have jobs? Before I take action to help someone get unemployment insurance benefits, I do all I can to help him get a job. I assume that the officials administering the Unemployment Insurance Act do all they can, but they only have the tools they are provided with. So, when someone after all is unemployed, they send him a notice stating he is disqualified because he has not been actively looking for work. They know at the UIC office that he cannot find work because there is none.
Manpower centres in the area know full well that the claimant cannot find a job because there is none available. He is disqualified just the same, and he loses the revenue toward which he had been contributing in the hope of receiving benefits until he could find a job. And if he insists, he is told to apply to the welfare office. In my province, welfare benefits are paid 50 per cent by the provincial government and 50 per cent by the federal government, while unemployment insurance is financed solely by the federal government. So they play games with the poor fellow who can have no more unemployment insurance benefits because he cannot find a job, but he is not told that he cannot find one because there is none. Far
from it, he is blamed for everything, and this is playing games with unfortunate people.
Mr. Speaker, even if someone wants a job for a few days or a few weeks, if an employer is willing to employ him for that period of time, the claimant would not dare take the risk for fear of getting into trouble. Most of the time claimants are not adequately informed of their rights, and often, through lack of information, they turn down offers of temporary employment.
He protests again and tells the Unemployment Insurance Commission that he does not understand why he was disqualified. He is then sent a notice telling him that he still has one possibility left open, an appeal to the board of referees. The board studies the case of this poor guy. They are not aware of all the details, and they are appointed ordinarily to do a job that comes under the jurisdiction of the government and they do not examine sufficiently the job opportunities in the area to know if the claimant is truly lazy and does not want to work or if he is not able to work.
That is the whole difference; there are those who want to work and those who do not want to do so. Being able to get a job and refusing it is not the same thing as not being able to find a job. The claimant is then told: "If you are not satisfied, you can appeal to the umpire. But for this, you need the authorization of the board of referees. You need the authorization of the chairman." But the chairman has decided that the poor boy is not entitled to benefits. He is the one to tell him: "It is true, you can appeal to the umpire or not." And if the decision of the umpire is not in the favour of the claimant, there is no other recourse. The case is closed. In other areas, you can still appeal to the Supreme Court. There are still some possibilities. Mr. Speaker, 1 would not want to close my comments without making some suggestions for improvement to the members of the House of Commons. I would not like my comments to be considered only as criticisms. This would not be in accordance with my true role.
There must be some change, and this according to the great formula of Major Douglas that is called the social credit, a credit which is more social and which serves everyone. He suggested that the community as a whole benefits entirely from the present inventions and progress as man is being replaced more and more by machines. We must find a formula that will enable society to receive an income earned by machines and progress. In our party we call this social credit, a credit which is distributed to the society because it is earned by machines and progress. We now have a different formula. Our politicians and political scientists have found another name for this. They call it guaranteed minimum annual income. Mr. Speaker, I do not care whether it is called a guaranteed minimum annual income formula or a national dividend formula, as long as we succeed in reaching our objective, that is the redistribution to all the workers of the income earned by machines if they have become unemployed because of those machines.

Mr. Speaker, I make this suggestion earnestly because I realize that the purpose of production is not only to produce for trade fairs or for the sake of production, but rather for consumption, in order to satisfy individual or community needs. If we make fire engines, it is to help municipalities fight fires in their area and not only to exhibit them.
Mr. Speaker, there are in our society some jobs which are guaranteed, which are secured. Those who hold these positions do not need unemployment insurance, but there are also jobs which are not guaranteed, which are available on a seasonal basis only, and those who fill them do need unemployment benefits. I wish we would take a consistent approach to enable these people whose job situation is not secure to rely on a guaranteed minimum annual income, without preventing them from earning money from another source. I find myself compelled to take part in this debate because he who doesn't speak out implies consent, and I certainly cannot associate myself with the remarks made by the opposition today. They have been either demagogic or simply election-minded, or even full of inconsistent jokes, accompanied by grotesque and disgraceful demonstrations as examplified by the member for Nickel Belt. Of course, I can only agree that unemployment is a sad situation and I am willing to associate myself with all those who accept to work positively and efficiently toward creating permanent jobs. To succeed in his task, we need the support of all economic agents in this country and even that of the opposition parties in this House.
Employment and Immigration
Today's debate is a blatant demonstration that there is a lot of empty chatter, a lot of common places, a lot of principles restated and the result of this situation is that when we are all tired of talking around, we will come to a vote and because the opposition will not have been responsible and efficient enough, Parliament will go on without solving anything. No one in this House should forget that he is a member of parliament and if he claims that Parliament should solve every problem he has but himself to blame for these shortcomings. With an opposition of the type we now have, the result would be an unsurpassed catastrophe. Of course I agree that the solution offered by Bill C-27 will not make my task any easier, nor improve the lot of certain of my constituents. If I accept the principles and the regulations spelled out in Bill C-27, it is because the excesses have reached such a state and are so many that I am led to conclude that the government would be unable to pay for them and so would the taxpaying workers. I cannot put off what can and should be done today. Giving Bill C-27 a six months' hoist would not resolve anything, and this is illustrated by the remarks of the hon. member for Roberval. He wants to delay discussion for six months, but to what avail? The hooded public servants he mentioned did not resolve anything, but what concerns me is not so much that public servants wear hoods, but that some hon. members also have them but are unaware of it. I would agree on a guaranteed minimum income, but I would not correct abuses by instantly creating another source of abuses.
Some hon. members have also talked about the zealous and interfering public official. What about hon. members who interfere with his work? As for imports, this is also a matter which can give rise to many lies. 1 am thinking about textiles. A glove factory in my constituency had to reduce its operations. We know that it costs $13.30 to produce a dozen of Canadian gloves whereas imported gloves cost $5.50. Will the opposition have the courage to tell the consumers that they want them to pay more? In the pulp and paper industry, everybody in the House knows it, Domtar has announced that they are going out of business in my constituency. How are we then to find a solution when we know that labour in East Angus is paid an hourly minimum wage of $6.61? Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on motion No. 4, I should like to qualify my position first of all by saying that I am diametrically opposed to what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has just told this House. We have got to put this situation into perspective. There was considerable debate at committee with respect to the question before us as a result of the amendment by the hon. member. In committee it was originally proposed by my colleague that the wording in the reprint of Bill C-17 dealing with contemplation of profit and the fact that Air Canada should be carried on with due respect for sound business considerations should come into Clause 6, making it
Air Canada
very clear that the corporation, within and outside Canada, should carry on business subject to those essential ingredients.
It should carry on in a sound business fashion in contemplation of profit.
It is rather interesting that it should be the House leader of the socialists who would be the first to become almost hysterical at the mere suggestion that we should have one of our Crown corporations operated in a sound fashion and in contemplation of profit. One of my colleagues from Winnipeg will be dealing more specifically with the disasters which have occurred under an NDP government out in Manitoba with the same type of philosophy the hon. member is asking us to accept for Air Canada tonight. I am sorry the hon. member did not attend the committee hearings when this matter was considered. If he had been there, even he would have been swayed a bit by some of the arguments placed by members on the government side as well as members from my party.
After the debate which occurred at committee, even the minister was willing to accept the amendment before us, provided it related only to the operation of the Board of Directors as opposed to the capacity of the company itself. That would have been the effect if the amendment was inserted in Clause 6.
Let us get matters into perspective. Let us realize what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has asked us to do in this House concerning Air Canada. Up to the present time Air Canada has had a $5 million capital. Most of the money used by Air Canada-and it is a billion dollar organization at the present time-has been loaned by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) on behalf of the people of Canada to Air Canada. It has been loaned at a nominal interest rate. Approximately $700 million of funds have been put into Air Canada, in addition to the $5 million of capital. The hard fact is that Air Canada has been running at a loss for the last three years. In fact, after 40 years of existence, Air Canada has total retained earnings of only $18 million as of today.
As further amendments are reached, I will put into evidence the contrast Air Canada's sad record has been over those 40 years compared to other airlines which it is competing with that have built up substantial retained earnings during the same period of time. speechtext:
The hon. member is asking what that has got to do with this amendment. Obviously he has not read the amendment. Tonight, tomorrow, or whenever this bill may be passed, we will authorize the government to put $750 million of our capital into Air Canada without even the suggestion of a commitment of a dividend or interest from Air Canada back to the public treasury. In short, it will be $750 million that can go into Air Canada with no further reference to this House.

July 19, 1977
Air Canada
In today's money cost at 10 per cent, it means in effect that Air Canada will be entitled to a subsidy of $75 million a year out of the pockets of the taxpayers of Canada, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has the audacity to stand up in the House and say it is wrong for us to propose an amendment which simply says that the directors, in the sleepy fashion in which they run Air Canada, should at least follow sound business practices and should try to make a profit.
Let us accept the facts. I have indicated that if we allow this bill to go through, $750 million will be the total capitalization that can be put into Air Canada, doing nothing. If Air Canada simply took that money and put it out at 10 per cent, it could make $75 million, and yet the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre tells us that, notwithstanding those facts, we should not expect it to make a profit, or we should not even hint to it that we would like it to carry on in contemplation of a profit.
Let us look at some of the evidence that was put forth in the committee hearings. For example, we were told that of the $750 million on a pro forma basis over the next five years, the government contemplates that only $370 million will actually be paid, in the form of paid in capital. I found it most interesting that there has been a misrepresentation with respect to the effect of that paid in capital. We have been told repeatedly that the reason the capitalization of Air Canada must be changed is that it has to be made vital and competitive with other airlines, that, in short, this capital is needed in order that Air Canada can somehow show a better profit picture over the coming years. We are simply saying in the amendment that if you intend to make a better profit over the coming years, then say so, write it into the act, let the succeeding boards of directors know at least that when this legislation was passed we in the House believed they should carry on their business in contemplation of profit.
The second thing I would like to point out is that not only do we feel they should carry on in contemplation of that profit but, what is rather remarkable, is that we had two pro forma statements furnished to us in committee. One showed what would happen to Air Canada if no financing change took place. Oddly enough we found that if no financing change should take place, the retained earnings as far as Air Canada is concerned, should be $70.7 million by 1981, but with the recapitalization, the retained earnings they contemplate would only be $69 million. In short, it makes virtually no difference.
The recapitalization that is being asked for by the minister, and which we have indicated should at least reflect a sizeable profit as far as the Air Canada pro forma statements are concerned, will in fact not result in greater retained earnings in 1981 than it would if the situation were left exactly as it is today. I think that is one thing, when we are considering the motion put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that we should bear in mind. Air Canada is in effect stating that this refinancing will have no net effect on its retained earnings between now and 1981, but the important thing is that it will have no net effect provided Air Canada
makes the money it contemplates it can make between now and 1981 which, contrary to what the socialists may think, means it has to make a profit. If it does not make that profit, the net result will be that the retained earnings between now and 1981 will be less for Air Canada and it will be the taxpayers of Canada who will have given the party. They in turn will be drained by an indirect subsidy in the form of free capital to the tune of possibly $60 million, $70 million, or $75 million in the form of lost interest.
That is why I believe, after having heard the sad tale of how Crown corporations are being operated in this country, how AECL lost $290 million last year alone, how virtually every Crown corporation which this government has ever had the responsibility to run has been a disaster, that when we are considering the recapitalization of an airline such as Air Canada we should say, fine, if you need this raw capital you should agree to carry on Air Canada in accordance with sound business principles and in contemplation of profit.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have asked for the opportunity to speak tonight in the adjournment debate on a subject that has been of great concern to me from the time I first campaigned in the riding of Kootenay West, that is, the economic development, or lack of it, of both the Kootenays. Recently we witnessed the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) signing several agreements with the province of B.C., the first time that any substantive agreement has been signed by the government with that province since 1974.
My concern is that in terms of the general development agreement which provides the overview and the basic thrust as to how economic assistance will be provided to that province there are three areas within that framework of the general development agreement that are clearly singled out and designed for special attention. We have the northeast part of British Columbia, the northwest part of British Columbia and the Kootenays.
I was very disturbed and disappointed, when I reviewed the various agreements which had been signed, to note that the assistance under the Regional Development Incentives Act specifically earmarked for Kootenay West was not renewed on December 31, 1975. It had not in fact again been put in place. Certainly it has been put in place for the northeast and the northwest, and I do not deny that there is a need. However, it seems to me that the other areas, particularly the Kootenays, earmarked in the GDA have not been identified.
If we look at all the agreements we find that they are applicable to all parts of British Columbia except for the lower mainland and southern Vancouver Island and except for those areas earmarked under the RDIA. I note, for example, that $5 million in assistance has been earmarked for small enterprise. I
Adjournment Debate
must say that I am very disappointed when 1 look at the figures. We see $30,000 for small businesses, but we see that they are limited in that they cannot have a capitalization of greater than $60,000. What can be done to expand or establish a new industry with that kind of financing? Whether it is a grant, a loan or whatever, it simply is not going to be effective.
I would like to move on to my specific concern. I have difficulty in finding any specific reference to Castlegar. Cas-tlegar has a potential for 150 new homes tomorrow. It will have a potential of 150 new jobs as soon as Can Cel expands. Castlegar is a bedroom community for the city of Trail. We will witness an expansion of the Cominco operations at Trail, costing some $425 million over the next six or seven years and employing 400 or 500 people for that period of time, and there are no accommodations. Why do we not have accommodations, and why can the industrial potential of Castlegar not be realized? Transportation is available, skilled workers are available, and everything else which is needed, except water, is available.
The Columbia River is right at Castlegar's doorstep, but the only way in which that community is going to be provided with potable water, and the only way that community is going to thrive, expand and realize its economic potential, is with proper provision for funding under the DREE program and under CMHC and with federal assistance and municipal participation. The municipality is prepared to carry its share of the load, but the only way it is going to survive is with a proper combination of those elements. The minister has indicated to me that there is provision under the new agreements which have been signed for that very specific problem, a very severe and acute problem which will shut down the industrial potential and the economic development of that community. It will also severely affect the livelihood of its citizens. I am pleased that the minister feels that there is potential within the agreement to provide that particular assistance, but quite frankly, I find it couched in such general and vague terms that I have difficulty in believing-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 6 the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco) asked a question as to the scope of subsidiary agreements being signed with the province of British Columbia. 1 am pleased to remind all members of this House of the signing, on July 8, of two agreements between our department and the province of British Columbia. These agreements provide a vehicle for coordinating and highlighting ongoing programs of the federal and provincial governments which are concerned with creating opportunities in the industrial sector, in agriculture and, more generally, in the rural areas of British Columbia.
The Canada-British Columbia Industrial Development Subsidiary Agreement identified areas of potential development within the province, recognizing the heavy dependence on export markets, the relatively narrow industrial base concern

July 19, 1977
Adjournment Debate
trated in small businesses and on resource activities such as forestry and mining. This agreement will provide $110 million in funding to assist in the diversification and distribution of economic activity throughout British Columbia. It will also provide for a large range of programs, including financial incentives and loans for small enterprises, financial support for industrial parks, and infrastructure and support for industrial commissions. In addition our department has also recently designated a large area in northern British Columbia for eligibility under DREE's regional development incentives program.
Under the Agriculture and Rural Development Subsidiary Agreement, the federal and provincial governments have committed themselves to programs expected to result in the expenditure of $87 million over the next five years to increase opportunties and employment in rural areas and encourage increased agricultural production. Sixty million dollars of this will be cost-shared between the two governments, while the remainder will be provided from the private sector.
When the hon. member for Kootenay West asked whether assistance for the water problem being experienced by Castle-gar and district can be provided under these agreements, I can only indicate that the new initiatives are sufficiently broad so as to enable the province and my department to provide assistance to areas outside the lower mainland-southern Vancouver Island areas, whenever projects can be accommodated within the stated objectives. With respect to the situation at Castlegar, I understand that officials of our department in Victoria and provincial officials are continuing to co-operate with municipal representatives in an effort to identify possible federal and provincial programs that might provide assistance. It is possible that assistance might be considered under the newly signed industrial agreement, but only if it can be related to infrastructure needs of an industry and in some way meets the objectives and criteria of the agreement.
I would indicate to the hon. member that years of study, together with months of discussion and negotiation, have produced these two agreements. Together, they represent both a good example of federal-provincial co-operation and a new emphasis on economic development in British Columbia. For the Department of Regional Economic Expansion they represent an important additional step along the road defined by our legislative mandate, which is to tackle regional disparities wherever in Canada they are encountered and, to a very large extent, in co-operation with the provincial governments.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this evening I raise once more the question of the appointment of territorial mining inspectors, a matter of great importance to those who work in the mines of the Northwest Territories. I raised this question on June 29 but did not receive a satisfactory answer. I directed it on June 30 to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand) but did not

receive a satisfactory answer then, either. I asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro (Hamilton East)) a question on June 14 about the appointment of inspectors in the Northwest Territories and was assured that my important questions would be answered. I am not satisifed with the government's non-answer to my question.
Surely I need not emphasize how important to people who work in the mines in the Northwest Territories is the appointment of mining inspectors who are concerned with the health and safety of miners. This concern is understandable because the mortality rate of miners in the Northwest Territories is very high.
As a result of this concern, and because the miners in the Northwest Territories do not feel the present federal mining inspectors are doing a competent job, the United Steelworkers Union got in touch with the territorial government, asking it to enforce the territorial mining safety ordinance by appointing territorial inspectors. This request was made to the commissioner at a meeting which took place on February 14, this year. The union received the assurance that this would be done.
Having heard nothing, the union wrote to the commissioner on May 25 this year, to learn what had happened. The commissioner wrote back on May 30 this year saying that he had written to the federal government on February 15, 1977, asking for authority to appoint territorial mine inspectors. He also informed that local of the United Steelworkers Union in the Northwest Territories that he had been trying for several years to get such authority but his efforts had not met with success.
That local of the United Steelworkers Union received, on June 8 this year, a letter from the office of the Minister of Labour. The letter said categorically that this matter does not come under the jurisdiction of the Department of Labour.
Quite apart from any question to do with mine safety and the appointment of inspectors to enforce safety standards, there seems to be some confusion in this area. Whose responsibility is it? The commissioner says it is not his responsibility. The Minister of Labour says it is not his. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development does not seem quite certain whose responsibility it is.
Again I ask the government to give the commissioner of the Northwest Territories authority to appoint mining inspectors. If it has already approved this, made some move toward it, or is ready to do so, why has it not notified the commissioner of this very important decision?
These are simple requests, although they deal with a very serious issue. There is no way that such a matter should drag on for months and months. I am quite sure that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the Minister of Labour and the government generally know of this issue because there have been many letters going back and forth.
I have raised this matter in the House three times, this being the third time. It is about time the government came forward
July 19, 1977

with some kind of answer to clarify the matter. There are lives at stake, and the health of many people who work in the mines. It is about time the government had an answer.
I now give the government another opportunity to answer to the people of Canada, and in particular the people of the Northwest Territories, as to what is the decision. Where are they now? May 1 ask the minister that?

subtopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS-ENFORCEMENT OF MINE SAFETY   REGULATIONS IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON CONSULTATION WITH MINISTER OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) first raised this question with the minister on June 29, he gave the impression that the responsibility for enforcing the mining safety ordinance was with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro). However, Northwest Territories Mining Safety and Rules is a territorial ordinance, the enforcement of which is presently the responsibility of the Yellowknife Engineering and Mine Inspection Unit of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
On February 15, 1977 Commissioner Hodgson wrote the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand) suggesting that mine inspection responsibilities be transferred to the territorial government effective September 1, 1977. His request was in response to a letter from the United Steelworkers of America, one of reportedly numerous requests made over the years from various mining related bodies in the Northwest Territories that the territorial government become actively involved in enforcing the Mining Safety Ordinance.
On May 25, 1977, the union again wrote to the commissioner inquiring as to the progress of his decision with respect to their proposal that the territorial government assume the responsibilities of mine inspection stating they are "ready to nominate suitable candidates for the new positions as they are established".
The request has been reviewed by officials both in Ottawa and in the field and the minister feels that the proposed transfer should be viewed positively.
However, the proposed transfer will affect the lives of many people. The views of mine workers, unions, mine management, territorial government and the department must be considered as to the effectiveness and the personnel implications of such a transfer. To be of any value, the proposed transfer must provide the Northwest Territories with a mining inspection service which better serves the mine workers and thus ultimately mine management.
In view of the fact that the busy summer season is now in full swing, it would appear that a complete study of the situation could not be made and a final decision taken in order for a transfer to take place by the September 1 deadline suggested by Commissioner Hodgson.

The question had to do with the new home insulation program which is now being extended to eight other provinces of Canada. I am not referring to the program which applies to Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, but a lesser discriminatory program for the other eight provinces. -all provinces have been briefed on the details of the home insulation program and are generally supportive of it.

minutes at my disposal. The hon. gentleman's statement has been repudiated by the minister of mines and energy in Newfoundland. The minister has answered this question a few times and 1 am wondering why the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) did not pay attention to those answers which the minister has already given on this subject.
Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island are heavily dependent on imported oil for electrical generation, to the extent of 63 per cent in the one case and in the other case 100 per cent. In all other provinces except New Brunswick oil is used to generate less than 7 per cent of the electricity consumed in those provinces. Accordingly, electricity prices in these two provinces are much more directly tied to oil price increases than is the case in other provinces, and in the last two years electricity prices have escalated at a dramatic rate. In order to minimize the impact of the higher prices the federal government decided to institute an insulation assistance program which would result in a reduction in the over-all energy bill of householders in the two provinces. This approach was adopted rather than instituting a subsidy to maintain artificially low
July 19, 1977

electricity prices because of the need to provide a continuing benefit to householders.
Other provinces, while also faced with higher oil prices, have not experienced the same increase in electricity prices. Accordingly a somewhat lower, but still substantial, level of subsidy will be made available to those provinces.
While there are differences between the national program and that available in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, the minister has explained why these differences exist. The Canadian home insulation program, with its major benefits to
